title: A day of kindness
tomorrow: praised at noon, blamed by five. how do you stay level?

lines: A HAND ON THE ELEVATOR DOOR.
FOUR WAYS THAT HOLD PEOPLE TOGETHER.
cards: A hand on the elevator door so it doesn't close on someone. A coffee order said back with a smile. The coworker who refills the paper tray before it runs out.
None of it gets posted anywhere. So, a kind act every hour: what even counts? The Buddha gave a short list that fits in a pocket.
And treating people as equals, the same with everyone. Four ways, he says, that hold people together.

teach.h: THE LINCHPIN OF A MOVING CART.
teach.b: The sutta ends on an object. These four, it says, are like the linchpin of a moving cart. A linchpin is a little pin pushed through the end of an axle so the wheel can't slide off.
Small enough to lose in a pocket. Pull it out, and the cart rolls on for a bit, then the wheel wobbles loose. That's the picture: things roll on small kindnesses.
The verse goes further than you'd expect.

teach.h: EVEN PARENTS' HONOR RESTS ON IT.
teach.b: Without these four, it says, not even a mother or a father would receive the honor their children owe them. Now the four, on a workday. Giving: half your fries, a pen, the good chair.
Kind speech: the warm hello, the true compliment, the thank-you said out loud. Helpful action: carrying the box, clearing the jam, the thing nobody asked you to do.
And the fourth, in Pali samanattata: being the same with everyone. The same voice for the boss and the cleaner. The same patience in the first hour and the eighth.
So every hour isn't a stopwatch. It's a pin you keep checking, because the wheel is always turning.

how: The four bases of sympathy (sangaha-vatthu) are taught to lay Buddhists as everyday ethics for home and work: giving, kind speech, helpful action and impartiality.

games.q: what does “a day of kindness” mean?
o: a day held together by small, steady kindnesses
a single grand favor, done once a year
a day spent only on yourself, to recharge

games.q: the four ways on a workday — tap the pairs.
p: half your fries, a pen, the good chair
the thing nobody asked you to do

s: the four ways only count if they're big gestures
the sutta compares them to a linchpin: small, and the wheel stays on.
the sutta compares these four to the linchpin of a moving cart
pull the pin and the wheel works loose; small acts hold things together.
the verse says even parents' honor rests on these four
without them, it says, not even a mother or father would receive the honor their children owe them.

games.q: hour six of your shift. the new hire asks the same question again, just as the manager walks in. what fits samanattata?
o: answer the new hire in the same patient voice you'd use for the manager.
turn to the manager first; the new hire can wait a few minutes.
stop answering. kindness every hour doesn't mean being a doormat.
games.why: samanattata is being the same with everyone: the same voice for the boss and the new hire, in the first hour and the sixth.

practice: Find something small within reach: a paperclip, a hair tie, a key. Hold it in your palm and feel how little it weighs; let it be the linchpin. With each slow breath, name one small kindness that could fit in your next hour.

wordCard.voice: A day of kindness: an ordinary day held together by small acts. Giving, kind words, help, and the same face for everyone.

orig.note: Pali: the bases of sympathy, the four ways that hold people together (AN 4.32).

carryVoice: The line to keep: every hour, small as a linchpin, and the wheel stays on. Day twenty-seven of thirty.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 4.32, Sangaha Sutta (the four bases of sympathy: giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, impartiality; like the linchpin of a moving cart; without them mother and father would not receive honor from their children)
